title: Go forth (Genesis 12:1–9)
hook: Abram, seventy-five, leaves his country for a land God will show him
carry: go, and I will show you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Babel: a tower to make a name, and a scattering. Your line was not our name. Did you manage one good thing with no credit? Today, God promises a name to one man. Day three hundred forty-five.

Most people at seventy-five are settling in. The house is paid off, or close. The grandkids, if there are any, live nearby. You know the pharmacist by name. Now picture someone that age packing everything onto animals, saying goodbye to the town where his father died, and heading out with no address. Not a retirement village. Not a place he's seen in photos. Just a direction, and a voice that said go. After eleven chapters about the whole world, Genesis suddenly zooms in on one old man, and the rest of the Bible flows from his first step.
screen: `SEVENTY-FIVE, AND SETTLED.` → `PACKING WITH NO ADDRESS.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, THEN ONE MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the call. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall shew thee." Three circles to leave, each one closer than the last: country, kindred, father's house. And one thing in exchange: a land God hasn't named yet. Which I shall show thee. The map comes after the step. In Hebrew, go forth is lekh lekha, and some Jewish teachers hear it as go to yourself, as if leaving home were also a way of becoming who you are. Second, the promise. I will make of thee a great nation, God says, and make thy name great. Notice the echo. At Babel, people tried to make a name for themselves. Here, God gives one. And then the widest line: in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Not just Abram's family. Everyone. Third, the response. Genesis doesn't record a word from Abram. It just says he went, as the Lord had told him. He was seventy-five. He took Sarai, his nephew Lot, and everything they had, and walked to Canaan, and built altars along the way. Fourth, how the Church remembers him. The Letter to the Hebrews says Abraham went out not knowing where he was going. The Catechism calls him the father of all who believe, and at Mass, the first Eucharistic Prayer names him our father in faith. Faith, for Catholics, starts here: not with knowing the whole map, but with a first step.
screen: `COUNTRY, KINDRED, FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `THE MAP COMES AFTER THE STEP.` · `GOD GIVES THE NAME.` · `ABRAM WENT, AT SEVENTY-FIVE.` · then, large: `GO FORTH OUT OF THY COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step without the full map. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that's waiting on you to have it all figured out first: a conversation, a change, an application, a call you keep not making. Notice how much of the map you want before you'll move. Now ask a smaller question: what's the first step, just the first? Picture yourself taking it. Not the whole road. One step. If you pray, you can ask God to show the next part when it's time. The bell holds the time.
Go forth. Lekh lekha in Hebrew: God's call to Abram to leave his country for a land not yet shown. He went, at seventy-five.
Your line: go, and I will show you. Today, take the first step you pictured, before you feel ready, and let the next one wait. Day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics call Abraham their father in faith; he is named in the Roman Canon at Mass, and the call of Abram (Genesis 12:1–4) is read on the Second Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle.

fork.setup: you're Abram, seventy-five. a voice tells you to leave your country, your kin and your father's house, for a land it hasn't named yet. what do you do?
options: ask to see the land first.
go, as the Lord told you.
fork.reveal: Genesis gives no speech: Abram went, as the Lord had told him, with Sarai, Lot and everything they had.

original.note: Hebrew: go forth, literally go for yourself. Jewish tradition names this part of Genesis by these words.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man moves house.
what it means: a call to leave everything for a place not yet shown, and a promise of blessing for every family on earth.
what a scholar hears: lekh lekha, go for yourself; God gives Abram the great name Babel tried to build.

sources.quoted: And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall shew thee.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 12:1 quoted from memory; confirm wording and 'shew'.
12:3 paraphrased as 'in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed'; the Douay-Rheims reads 'kindred'. Kept unquoted. Confirm.
Lekh lekha as 'go to yourself' (e.g. Rashi reads 'for your benefit'; Hasidic readings 'go to yourself'). Stated as 'some Jewish teachers'. Confirm.
Roman Canon: the current English Missal names Abraham 'our father in faith'; paraphrased. Confirm.
howItsDone: Genesis 12:1–4a is the first reading for Lent II, Year A; confirm.
